This was reported on Monday by the online portal Risky Business. According to the report, the attacker first gained access to the National Agency for Cadastre and Real Estate Advertising ANCPI (Agenția Națională de Cadastru și Publicitate Imobiliară), the country's land registry authority, and later attempted to sell the stolen data in specialized internet forums. Continue after ad As Risky Business reported , citing unnamed sources, the cybercriminal gained access to the ANCPI database with valid credentials and explored the internal systems. After the extortion of the authority failed, he finally deleted all systems and backups, according to his statements. According to the online portal Cybernews , the attacker boasted in the Dark Web that he had manipulated backup copies of the stolen data to prevent their recovery. The Romanian Land Registry initially spoke of technical problems but then had to admit to being the victim of a cyberattack. The incident became public on July 14. One day later, some stolen ANCPI data were offered for sale in a relevant internet forum, including access data of employees, internal documents, and details about the authority's IT network. Real estate market grinds to a halt The deletion of the land registry database, in turn, brought the entire Romanian real estate market to a standstill, according to Risky Business. Official apps and websites of the authority have been offline since the cyberattack. Notaries can currently not certify new transactions, and citizens can neither retrieve proof of ownership nor detailed land registry excerpts. “Currently, the ANCPI's IT infrastructure is undergoing a comprehensive process of reinstallation and consolidation,” the authority writes in a press release . “The authority's technical teams, together with cybersecurity specialists, are implementing measures for recovery, verification, and strengthening of protective measures so that services can be resumed under conditions of maximum security.” Contrary to some information circulating in public, the ANCPI has several backup copies of its systems; the authority further stated, “a measure that ensures redundancy and enables data recovery in the event of cybersecurity incidents.” Videos by heise mehr Videos c't 3003 heise & ct Peertube Meanwhile, a cybersecurity firm has identified the criminals behind the cyberattack. The stolen data was reportedly published by an account called “ByteToBreach.” Earlier this year, this account is suspected of having already penetrated the Swedish e-government portal and possibly numerous state registers in Eastern Europe, including in Slovakia, Ukraine, Poland, and Lithuania. The cybersecurity company KELA assumes that the criminal Zakaria Mahdjoub from Oran (Algeria) is behind “ByteToBreach.” According to Risky Business, experts describe him as a “technically skilled cybercriminal who sells sensitive global data from airlines, banks, and governments.” Continue after ad ( akn ) Don't miss any news – follow us on Facebook , LinkedIn or Mastodon . Photograph: Cheng Chia Huang/Getty Images View image in fullscreen A tactical military exercise in Tainan, Taiwan, 2026. Photograph: Cheng Chia Huang/Getty Images Politics books Review War Is Interested in You by Gideon Rachman review – are we on the brink of world war three? A foreign affairs expert’s bleak assessment of the state of global security Charlie English Mon 26 Oct 2026 05.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A re we on the brink of a new world war? This bleak subject is increasingly invoked by leaders, soldiers and officials, from Donald Trump to Vladimir Putin to the heads of our military and intelligence services. It’s an urgent theme, then, for the FT foreign affairs columnist Gideon Rachman to explore in his latest survey of global diplomacy. Rachman draws his title from the expression, sometimes attributed to Trotsky: “You may not be interested in war, but war is interested in you” – the idea being that conflict doesn’t much care whether we like to think about it or not: it will come knocking on our doors regardless. Clearly, humanity is in a particularly unsafe spot right now, but seeing our security issues laid out like this, catalogued and mapped and analysed, they seem almost overwhelming. To summarise: the most powerful, nuclear-armed states – the US, China and Russia – are led by unscrupulous, self-dealing “strongmen”, each of whom is playing with the nationalist “Great Again” politics epitomised by Trump. Democracy is being rolled back around the world, and even bastions of liberalism such as the UK, France and Germany seem vulnerable to takeover by the Putin-friendly far right. The so-called rules-based international order and its institutions – the UN, the WTO, Nato – are being deliberately undermined by the aforementioned strongmen, and are as weak now as they have ever been. Of all the potential flashpoints, it is Taiwan that may offer the fastest route to a world war Putin has described the new world order with the term “might makes right”, and the result is that conflicts have been breaking out at a rate unprecedented in the postwar era. According to Rachman, there were 61 in 2024 alone, and 11 full-blown wars. This included Gaza as well as some conflicts far less visible in the west, such as the one in Sudan, which by mid-2025 had led to 150,000 battlefield deaths. In 2026 many “state-based conflicts” are ongoing, including the largest land war in Europe since 1945 (in Ukraine) and the most disruptive in the Middle East for more than 20 years (Iran). Although these are mostly confined to their regions, they have begun to overlap and spread, as Russia deploys North Korean troops and tests Nato’s resolve, Iran throttles global shipping, and Ukraine advises Gulf states on drone use. And even as these grind on, others threaten to explode, including between India and Pakistan, North and South Korea, and China and Taiwan. Of these potential flashpoints, it is Taiwan that may offer the fastest route to a world war, since it could bring China and the US into direct conflict. For decades, Taiwan’s security was guaranteed by US naval superiority; now Beijing, after a massive military buildup, has more warships than Washington. It’s said that the single Chinese shipyard on Changxing Island has more capacity than all US yards combined. Still, Xi Jinping knows that if the US comes to Taiwan’s aid, the result would be a bloodbath, which is why US presidents have mostly been keen to emphasise the US’s commitment to Taiwan. But Trump has been far more ambivalent – declaring in May this year, for instance, that “I think the last thing we need right now is a war that’s 9,500 miles away” – which only increases the risk of China attempting an assault. It’s here, in the shifting power balance between China and the US, that the root of the new global insecurity lies. Whatever you think of American hegemony, the US maintained a sort of stability, after the cold war, in which victims could plausibly appeal to international law. The 2003 invasion of Iraq destroyed that system, and US failure there and in Afghanistan persuaded future presidents against intervention. Three times, between 2012 and 2015, Obama chose not to step in to address illegal acts by the Assad regime, Russia and China, which signalled an American retrenchment. The Trump administration has taken this further, reverting to the kind of isolationist, tariff-based protectionism that postwar institutions such as the UN security council and WTO were built to avoid. It’s hard not to spot echoes here of the 1930s – the time, incidentally, when the slogan “America first” was popularised. How to offset these risks? Rachman surveys a handful of mechanisms that have helped maintain the peace, and finds them wanting. The rules-based international order, for instance, barely functioned in its heyday; now, as Mark Carney put it plainly, it “no longer works”: we are living through a “rupture”. What about spreading democracy and economic stability as a path to peace – a principle exemplified by the “Golden Arches” theory, which states that no two nations with McDonald’s will wage war on each other? There’s no comfort here either, as that was proved wrong in the 1990s, and the number of democracies has been declining steadily since 2006. Then there’s deterrence, which still by and large keeps us safe. But it hasn’t stopped fighting between nuclear-armed India and Pakistan, and China and North Korea are rapidly expanding their atomic arsenals. What we’re left with, then, as American primacy declines, is a global version of Trump’s “Donroe doctrine”, in which each major power gets a “sphere of influence” where they call the shots. In this scenario, Washington rules over the Americas, Beijing over east Asia, and Moscow the old Soviet zone. Clashes are sorted out by one-to-one conversations between authoritarian leaders. But what if these rulers fall out? And anyway, who wants to live in the shadow of an overbearing neighbour? While the outlook of War Is Interested in You is undoubtedly gloomy, Rachman’s book is not. His writing is engaging and anecdotal, and he brings vast experience to bear on a vital subject. He won’t go so far as to say a new world war is inevitable, but the threat is becoming impossible to ignore. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Bookmarks Discover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. https://telex.hu/ugynokaktak/2026/11/09/.text: Szükséges, hogy felajánlotta a lemondását a főigazgató, de a miniszteri szintű felelősség, magának a miniszterelnöknek a felelőssége is felmerül – mondta Apáti István, a Nemzetbiztonsági Bizottság mi hazánkos elnöke a bizottság hétfői ülése , majd az utána tartott nyilvános egyeztetés után. Az egyeztetésen Cseh Gergő Bendegúz, az Állambiztonsági Szolgálatok Történeti Levéltárának (ÁBTL) elnöke felajánlotta lemondását . Apáti azt mondta, nem a tiszás tagokat hibáztatja azért, hogy nem mentek el az ülésre. Inkább magát a miniszterelnököt, aki rendre hangoztatja, mennyire fontos, hogy mindennek legyen következménye a politikában, ennek ellenére azt a korábban a Fidesz által alkalmazott módszert használta, hogy a kormánypárti képviselők távolmaradása miatt határozatképtelenné tette az ülést. „Akinek nincs takargatnivalója, eljöhetett volna” – mondta a mi hazánkos politikus, aki szerint „a hivatali visszaélés előszobája” az, hogy a végrehajtó hatalom, vagyis a kormány beleszól az egyik legfontosabb bizottság munkájába. „Ez történik, ha az ország vezetői a tűzre nem vizet, hanem 100-as benzint visznek” – mondta Apáti arról, hogy a nyitottaktak.hu adatbázisában korábban többen is megfigyelőként voltak feltüntetve, pedig őket figyelték meg, ez történt Lezsák Sándorral is . Apáti felvetette, hogy az Alkotmányvédelmi Hivatal (AH) felelősségét is vizsgálni kéne az ügynökakták nyilvánosságra hozatalában. Hegedűs Barbara, a bizottság fideszes tagja is felsőbb szinten, nem csak a levéltár vezetésében keresné a felelősöket azért, hogy a levéltár kereshető adatbázisában a megfigyeltek nevei is szerepeltek. Ő is felvetette a miniszterelnök felelősségét az ügyben, ragaszkodott ahhoz, hogy a politikai felelősöket kell felelősségre vonni, mert a levéltár a lehető legjobb munkát végezte a szoros határidő betartása mellett. Bejelentette azt is, hogy a Fidesz parlamenti vizsgálóbizottság felállítását kezdeményezi az ügyben. A Telex ügynökakták mellékletét a Telex a Szabad Sajtóért Közhasznú Alapítvány támogatja.

https://www.nwaonline.com/news/2026/nov/.text: Berlin Wall pieces go on display in northeast Arkansas’ National Cold War Center BLYTHEVILLE -- For decades, the Berlin Wall marked the dividing line between Communist oppression and freedom. Now, three dozen segments of the infamous barrier belong to the National Cold War Center in Blytheville. At a gala dinner Saturday evening, the gray, concrete behemoths went on display for the first time. It's "the largest collection of the Berlin Wall in the United States," said Christian Ostermann, the center's executive director. More than 600 people, including former Polish President Lech Walesa, attended the event, which was held inside Hangar 207, at the old Eaker Air Force Base. A Nobel Peace Prize winner and Solidarity trade union co-founder, Walesa was the face of resistance in his country for nearly a decade. Frequently fired and often jailed, the Gdansk shipyard worker helped usher in free and democratic elections in his homeland. In 1990, he became Poland's first popularly elected president. His rise to political power came months after the fall of the Berlin Wall. Speaking in downtown Blytheville Friday evening as part of the center's Cold War Week events, Walesa heaped praise on former President Bill Clinton. He did so again at Saturday's gala. "Thanks to him, we are in NATO and that is the real end of the Cold War," he said, a remark that drew applause. Before leaving, he endorsed the center's efforts. "I'm very happy that you're building your museum, and I certainly hope that you'll hurry up because I certainly want to be there when you open," Walesa, 83, said through a translator. "So I'll support you and help you every which way I can so that I can be at your opening." In an interview, Thomas F. "Mack" McLarty, who served as Clinton's first White House chief of staff, said the two heads of state "clearly were kindred spirits." "He and President Clinton were kind of soulmates, in some ways," McLarty said. "Walesa was visionary. He was bold. He had really serious, deep ideas about democracy and about involving people in leadership and security issues. I mean, he was a serious thinker and clearly still is." Saturday's crowd was in a festive mood, posing for photos in front of Berlin Wall segments and examining a Soviet-era Russian fighter jet. The center revealed that Lockheed Martin, a U.S. defense contractor with facilities in Camden and Fort Smith, has committed to making a $2 million donation. As Walesa headed toward the exits, he paused to take pictures with the women who had checked guests in, smiling broadly and greeting them all. "He's the president of Poland? Like, the country?" one of them asked. Former Gov. Asa Hutchinson, who serves on the National Cold War Center's national advisory board, gave Walesa's introduction. "He was a hero of mine as I was a young United States attorney under Ronald Reagan," Hutchinson said in an interview beforehand. "He changed history." The new museum is needed, Hutchinson said. "This is just critically important from a history standpoint and also from an economic standpoint for Arkansas, so I'm engaged in it," he said. Former Supreme Allied Commander Europe of NATO Wesley Clark, who is also on the center's advisory board, delivered the keynote address, describing himself as "a victim and a survivor of the Cold War." He recalled witnessing the beginnings of the space race as an eighth grader living in Little Rock, living through the Cuban missile crisis while studying at West Point and being wounded while serving in Vietnam. During the Cold War, "we had strength -- economic strength and military strength. But today, as a result of the peace dividend that we took in the early 1990s, we find ourselves under-strength to provide the protection to our friends and the extended deterrence abroad that our friends are looking for," he said. "Instead of a single threatening adversary like the Soviet Union, we're now facing a convergence of adversaries: Russia, China, North Korea and Iran, three nuclear armed, the fourth seeking nuclear weapons. So we need to remember we won this Cold War with strength," he said. These days, our allies are asking, "Where is the American leadership," he said. Though thousands of miles from Moscow, Eaker (formerly Blytheville) Air Force Base, played an important role during the Cold War. The site of a Strategic Air Command Center, it had nuclear weapons at the ready and planes on hand, prepared to fly if Armageddon came. The base closed in 1992, following the collapse of the Soviet Union. Since 2018, the Blytheville Air Force Base Strategic Air Command Alert and Weapons Storage Areas have been listed on the National Register of Historic Places. In 2023, Congress designated the museum in Blytheville as the official National Cold War Center. It has a collection of items related to the East-West conflict, including an old Soviet fighter jet and a towering statue of Vladimir Lenin. Now, it also has remnants of the conflict from the front lines. The concrete Cold War relics now in Blytheville had resided in recent years in a warehouse roughly two hours north of Berlin. Working with Berlin Wall Foundation Project Leader Cornelia Thiele, Ostermann and Barry Harrison, vice chairman of the center's board of directors, traveled to Germany earlier this year and selected some of the most colorful ones. A film crew accompanied them. A documentary about the adventure is being shot and will air on Arkansas TV, National Cold War Center officials announced Saturday evening. They hope to see it released next year. They're also working to raise $75 million to pay for construction and create an endowment. This was the seventh annual gala. Last year's event raised about $450,000, center officials said. Since then, momentum has been building, center officials said. "I really think this is the weekend that this thing (takes off) -- the snowball's going to start rolling down the hill. We're excited," Harrison said. The wall segments are evidence of the progress that has already been made. Moving the graffiti-scarred pieces was complicated. "We had help on both sides of the ocean," Harrison said. "They came through Savannah and then by train up here," Ostermann said. The entire journey took about a month. Each segment is about 12 feet high, 4 feet wide and weighs as much as a small elephant. "They're really heavy -- 2.6 tons each," Thiele said. Construction on an early version of the wall began in 1961. The segments in Blytheville are a later model, Ostermann said. "This is called Wall '75," he said. "There was a wall 2000 in the plans, in the works. Of course the wall didn't make it to 2000, fortunately." Some of the segments are pockmarked, the damage caused by what Ostermann and Thiele referred to as "wall peckers." "After the wall came down in 1989, people wanted to have souvenirs," Ostermann said. "You had hundreds of people chiseling away." Other people were eager to remove any reminders of the life under the East German regime. "At least 140 people died at the Berlin Wall trying to escape the country," Thiele said. Today, few pieces of the wall remain standing. The segments in Blytheville are in unusually good shape. Since the end of the Cold War, these segments had been shielded from the elements, Ostermann said. Farmers had used them to make towering concrete squares, filling the space in between with grain. Eventually, visitors will be able to see them on a regular basis. "We're working on an outdoor campus display, hopefully breaking ground sometime early next year," Ostermann said. Two years ago, center officials said the museum was scheduled for completion in late 2027. These days, they say the timeline will depend on their fundraising efforts. An update on the amount raised was not provided during Cold War Week. For now, visitors are able visit Building 202 on Idaho Street. When the base was still open, the 340th Bombardment Squadron had its headquarters there. Now, the 6,000-square foot facility houses the National Cold War Center's BAFB Exhibition. In addition to displaying artifacts, it tells the base's story, describes life during the Cold War and shows videos of veterans who served there. Mary Gay Shipley, who put her community on the literary roadmap when she owned and operated That Bookstore in Blytheville, is deeply involved in the effort, and serves as chair of the center's board of directors. She's convinced the museum is a winning idea. "I do believe this one's going to work," she said. "I think it has (a) potential that is greater than anything I've ever been involved in." Frank E. https://tert.am/en/news/2026/11/10/EU%20.text: USD - 360.35 -0.18 EUR - 395.09 -0.09 RUB - 4.39 -0.01 USD - 360.35 -0.18 Politics Economy Law Event Press digest Science/tech Sports Culture Entertainment Video Politics Economy Law Event Press digest Science/tech Sports Culture Entertainment About us Video EU budget battle erupts as four countries defy Merz over Ukraine aid The leaders of Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Bulgaria have pushed back against German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's ultimatum to make approval of the EU's next long-term budget conditional on fresh financial support for Ukraine. Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico denounced the move as a "textbook case of blackmail" and threatened to wield his veto. "We have an equal say in this matter," Fico said on Tuesday as he welcomed his Czech counterpart, Andrej Babiš, in Bratislava. "Just as Mr Merz talks about using his veto, I can say exactly the same. We have the same veto power as the German federal chancellor." Babiš quipped that Merz "probably doesn't realise" that the proposed EU budget already earmarks €100 billion for Ukraine. However, those funds will not become available until 2028, while Kyiv faces a €70 billion shortfall next year. "Today will not be business as usual – not by a long shot. Today, we must respond to blackmail," Fico said, expressing his displeasure. "What the federal chancellor is doing is a textbook case of blackmail, and I reject it. We are a sovereign country. We are the Slovak Republic. We have our own views."
